messages.content: Ты решаешь задачи. Если нужно посчитать или найти факт, вызывай инструменты, а не угадывай. Когда ответ готов, напиши его последней строкой в формате FINAL: <ответ>. Для числовых задач в FINAL только число, для вопросов о фактах короткая фраза. ВАЖНО про формат FINAL: отвечай на том же языке, на котором задан вопрос, и копируй формулировку максимально близко к найденному источнику - не переводи и не перефразируй. Если источник на английском, а вопрос тоже на английском (или явно про англоязычный факт), FINAL должен быть на английском, дословно как в источнике: имена, названия, цитаты - без перевода на русский. Для дат пиши в формате 'число месяц' без года, если год не спрашивают явно (например, '15 March', а не '15 март' и не 'March 15, 2026'). Для чисел с приставками (трлн/млрд/млн, T/B/M) используй ту же запись и тот же язык, что были бы уместны в источнике, не переводи единицы измерения. Если факт в источнике выражен как соотношение или с уточнением (например, '4 of 5', 'nine of 27'), приведи его в FINAL полностью, а не только первое число.

Last updated July 25, 2026. SpaceX Starship Flight 13 launched on July 24, 2026, succeeding on its primary objectives and deploying the first real Starlink V3 satellites into space. The suborbital mission concluded with the softest Starship splashdown yet in the Indian Ocean, marking a historic leap for the aerospace company. This 13th flight test of the SpaceX Starship, and the second flight of the Starship V3 configuration, utilized Super Heavy Booster 20 (B20) and Ship 40 (S40), standing approximately 407 feet tall at Orbital Launch Pad 2, SpaceX Starbase, Texas. By successfully demonstrating satellite deployment, in-space relight, and a controlled reentry, SpaceX has proven the core capabilities required for future operational and lunar missions. The road to the launch pad: The journey to this successful suborbital flight was not without its hurdles. The FAA officially closed the Flight 12 mishap investigation on July 13, 2026, clearing Flight 13 for liftoff. A second attempt on July 23 was scrubbed due to weather from Tropical Storm Bertha. Starship Deploys Starlink Satellites and Splashes Down Intact By Alan Boyle - July 24, 2026 11:59 PM UTC | Missions - 27K reads SpaceX's Starship launch system rises from its Texas launch pad for a suborbital flight test. (Credit: SpaceX via X) SpaceX's Starship super-rocket deployed operational next-generation Starlink satellites for the first time during its 13th flight test , which addressed snags that arose in the previous test. The 407-foot-tall, two-stage rocket rose from its Starbase launch pad in Texas at 5:51 p.m. CT today (10:51 p.m. UTC), with all 33 Raptor engines firing on the Super Heavy booster. On the way up, the rocket set a record for maximum dynamic pressure, also known as Max-Q. Minutes after liftoff, the Starship upper stage â known as Ship â separated to continue on the flight test's trajectory, and then the booster relit its engines for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot noted that not all of the engines fired up as planned â making for a splash that was a bit spicier than expected but still safe. During the next phase of the test, Ship sent out 20 operational Starlink V3 satellites from a deployment system that's been nicknamed the "Pez Dispenser." For about 20 minutes, SpaceX's engineering team ran a series of tests to check the deployment of solar arrays and see how the satellites were able to communicate with other spacecraft in the telecom network using laser systems. "Not only were we able to make contact with all 20, but we also made comms over lasers with all of them as well," SpaceX engineer Kate Tice said. "So, that is awesome."
